compare_blocks.body:
In this fictional pitch review, both people have the same materials, audience, time, equipment and authority. Each row compares possible emphases under the same conditions.

compare_blocks.body:
At a startup meeting, either person may take charge or wait to speak. Their role, decision authority and familiarity with the people in the room can all affect what they do.

The shared E describes where attention and energy tend to go. It does not measure how warm, confident or organised either person is.

The difference sits in three places, and each says one thing that cannot stand in for the others. S/N is where evidence comes from: given a document, do comparable fact and past experience get grabbed first, or the links between pieces of information and the overall direction. T/F is the standard of judgement: does weighing cite a standard that can be applied alike, or put the people involved and what they value into the call. J/P is the outward posture: is the arrangement and the conclusion settled first, or are options kept open for new information. ### ENTJ and ESFP: should the first slide carry a conclusion or a moment

Either person can suggest either edit. The order of information on a slide is a presentation decision. It cannot identify someone’s type.

If the audience already understands the product, spend more time on the decision it faces. If it is new to the product, a short demonstration can provide context. Either presenter can combine the demonstration with a clear request.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The most common misread sorts them by who is more outgoing or more articulate. Both may speak first in a silent room, and both may sit through an unfamiliar setting without a word. E describes the direction of attention, not volume; treating volume as type is wrong nearly every time.

The second sorts by profession and dress. Working in sales and dressing brightly does not make someone ESFP; working in strategy and speaking in jargon does not make someone ENTJ. Those impressions are mostly shaped by training, experience and the demands of a post: the same person in a different role, asked for a different register, looks like another style two years later.

Function order in this notation does not measure whether someone can structure a pitch or understand how it will land. Either skill can be developed.

The fourth takes a single action as the test. Which line gets cut, whether the deck changes on the spot, at what level an improvisation lands — any of these can be decided by the audience reaction, the product stage, who owns the final cut and how long is left before the pitch. The same person will choose oppositely in different settings, so one action carries no classificatory value.

compare_blocks.body:
